newsitem.title: USA: Simpson ends first round of civil trial testimony.
newsitem.headline: Simpson ends first round of civil trial testimony.

text.p: After three days of scathing interrogation, O.J. Simpson stepped down from the witness stand at his civil trial on Tuesday without a single question from his own attorney.

In a surprise tactical move, Simpson lead attorney Robert Baker, who had been expected to immediately begin his effort to "rehabilitate" his client in front of the jury, told Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki: "I'm sorry, your honour, I changed my mind."
But Baker promised to bring the former football star back to testify when the defence begins presenting its case in the wrongful-death lawsuit, possibly as early as next month.

With that, the trial was recessed for a long Thanksgiving holiday break. Testimony resumes next Tuesday when the plaintiffs will put on more witnesses to support their claims that Simpson murdered his ex-wife and her friend.

The latest unexpected twist in the two-month trial came on the same day the judge dismissed a 25-year-old woman juror, an aspiring actress and singer, for misconduct after she was accused of trying to contact attorneys in the case.

Simpson's testimony marked the dramatic high point of the trial, in which he is fighting civil charges brought by the families of murder victims Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman. He was acquitted of double-murder charges in a criminal trial in October of last year.
Taking the witness stand in open court for the first time since the 1994 killings, Simpson spent three days being grilled relentlessly about inconsistencies in his story.

Simpson repeatedly maintained his innocence as he fended off harsh accusations, but he never lost his cool. He conceded, however, he was at a loss to explain how he cut his hand, how blood matching his own ended up at the murder scene and how blood matching the victims ended up in his Ford Bronco and at his Brentwood estate.

And in his first round of testimony, Simpson made no mention of the controversial theory that is expected to form the centrepiece of Simpson's defence -- that he was framed by a police conspiracy orchestrated by a racist detective.
Baker had been expected to bring that out under friendly cross-examination Tuesday. Instead, he told the judge: "We'll do our whole questioning of him when we put on our case."
Simpson's abrupt departure from the witness stand means jurors begin the holiday recess with a final image of the former football star fending off harsh attacks.

But some legal analysts called it a sound tactical move. "The obvious logic is to put him on the stand and surround him with friendly witnesses later," said Loyola University Law School professor Laurie Levenson.

Attorneys for the victims' families concluded their interrogation by directly accusing Simpson of murder. "In fact, you murdered Nicole, didn't you?" asked John Kelly, who represents Nicole Brown Simpson's estate.
"That's absolutely false," Simpson replied calmly.
"And you murdered Ron," Kelly continued.
"That's absolutely wrong," Simpson said, looking directly at the jury."

Under questioning by the plaintiff's attorneys, Simpson again denied that he had ever beaten his ex-wife but said he felt at times like a "battered husband" because of the abuse he claimed to have suffered at her hands.
The families' attorneys contend that Simpson beat, stalked and terrorised his ex-wife during their 17-year relationship and finally killed her when he could no longer control her.

At the start of Tuesday's session, the judge said he had dismissed a juror for "communicating with or attempting to communicate with persons connected with this case." In announcing his decision, he admonished the remaining panellists that "a jury is not a social club."

The woman, Ann-Marie Jamison, had been variously described in news reports as white, Hispanic and of mixed white and Hispanic heritage. She was replaced by a young white woman, bringing the jury's racial makeup to nine whites, one black, one Hispanic and one Asian- black.
